title: UK Moves Toward New Maritime Fuel Standard
summary: The UK's Department for Transport is consulting on a "new" maritime fuel standard for 2030, suspiciously mirroring the EU's FuelEU Maritime for ships over 5,000 GT. Despite claims of emissions reduction, the proposed "flexibility mechanisms"—pooling, banking, and borrowing—offer familiar loopholes for avoiding tangible decarbonization. With implementation a distant 2030 and key emission reduction targets still undefined, this 'consultation' offers little immediate assurance against excessive carbon intensity or HFO usage.
content:
The United Kingdom has launched a consultation on new maritime fuel regulations that could require thousands of ships calling at British ports to progressively reduce the greenhouse gas emissions intensity of their fuels beginning in 2030.

The Department for Transport’s proposal, published Monday, November 16, would establish a fuel standard broadly aligned with the European Union’s FuelEU Maritime regulation while leaving room for adjustments as international negotiations at the International Maritime Organization (IMO) continue.

Under the government’s preferred approach, the rules would initially apply to ships of 5,000 gross tonnage and above, regardless of flag, covering approximately 5,000 vessels based on historical port-call data.

The proposed framework would regulate all energy used on domestic voyages between UK ports, 50% of energy used on international voyages to and from the UK, and energy consumed by covered ships while at berth in British ports.

Rather than mandating particular fuels, the regulation would establish progressively tightening limits on the lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions intensity of energy consumed by ships. Operators could meet those requirements through alternative fuels, electrification and other lower-emission energy sources.

The government is also considering compliance flexibility mechanisms, including pooling, banking and borrowing emissions credits, similar to provisions under FuelEU Maritime.

However, several important details remain undecided, including how quickly emissions limits would tighten and whether the UK should follow the EU’s trajectory, align with future IMO standards or establish its own targets.

The government expects the regulation to take effect from 2030.

Industry Welcomes Consultation, Warns of Practical Challenges

The UK Chamber of Shipping welcomed the consultation but urged policymakers to ensure that new requirements reflect the availability of alternative fuels, supporting infrastructure and commercially viable technologies.

“We welcome the Government moving forward with this consultation. Greater long-term certainty can help unlock the investment needed to decarbonise shipping, but regulation needs to develop alongside the fuels, infrastructure and technology that operators will need,” a Chamber spokesperson said.

“Any future UK framework must be practical, support investment and maintain the international competitiveness of UK shipping.”

The Chamber has previously called for a regulatory framework that avoids duplicating existing international requirements while providing operators with sufficient flexibility to manage the transition.

In an October policy paper, the organization recommended aligning fuel certification and lifecycle emissions accounting with emerging IMO standards, developing reliable monitoring and verification systems, and setting targets based on realistic assessments of fuel availability and infrastructure readiness.

Those concerns are particularly relevant given the significant overlap between ships trading to the UK and those already subject to European regulations.

According to the government’s consultation, approximately 97% of ships above 5,000 gross tonnage that called at UK ports in 2019 also called at EU ports.

UK Presses Ahead Amid IMO Uncertainty

The consultation comes as the international shipping industry continues to grapple with uncertainty surrounding the IMO’s proposed global Net-Zero Framework.

While the UK government acknowledges that international regulation remains the most effective way to reduce shipping emissions, it argues that uncertainty over global measures should not prevent domestic action.

The proposed fuel regulation would complement the UK’s existing maritime carbon-pricing measures, including the extension of the UK Emissions Trading Scheme to domestic shipping in July 2026.

The government is also seeking industry feedback on whether smaller ships should eventually be included, with vessels between 400 and 5,000 gross tonnage remaining under review.

Beyond the emissions requirements themselves, the consultation examines the availability of alternative maritime fuels, bunkering infrastructure, port readiness and the investment needed to support widespread adoption.

The Department for Transport has emphasized that its proposals are preliminary and that no final regulatory decisions have been made.

The consultation remains open until February 22, 2027.

The UK Chamber of Shipping said it will work with its members and the UK Alternative Maritime Fuels Coalition to develop a detailed response addressing the operational, commercial and technical implications of the proposed framework.
